opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the "policy" isn't just the model weights. That's where a lot of people get tripped up. When we say we want the agent to recursively self-improve, we mean the whole system that decides what to do next: the underlying model, the scaffolding around it, the prompts, the tools it can call, the memory it keeps, and the evaluation loop that tells it whether it did well.

If you only think of the policy as weights, self-improvement means "go retrain yourself," and that's slow, expensive, and hard to verify. But much of what makes an agent good in practice is outside the weights. It's how it breaks down a task, which tools it picks, how it recovers when something fails, what it remembers from last time. All of those are things the agent can inspect and modify itself, often on a much faster cycle.

So conceptually, the policy is a program, and some of that program is learned parameters and some is explicit structure. The recursive part is that the agent is allowed to propose changes to that program, test them against some signal it trusts, and keep the ones that actually help. Then the improved version is the one proposing the next round of changes.

The hard part, and honestly where most of the interesting research is, is the signal. Self-improvement is only as good as your ability to tell whether a change was an improvement. If your evaluation is noisy or gameable, the agent will happily optimize toward something you didn't want. So much of our thinking goes into making the feedback loop grounded: real tasks, real outcomes, verifiable results where possible, rather than the agent just grading its own homework.

And the last piece is keeping it legible. If the agent is rewriting parts of itself, you want those changes to be things a human can read and reason about, at least for now. That's another reason we like the framing of the policy as something broader than weights. Changes to a prompt, a tool, or a workflow are much easier to audit than a diff of a billion parameters.

r001.rationale: It describes policy as the model plus surrounding scaffolding, prompts, tools, and memory, but does not clearly characterize an agent as an LM call wrapped in machinery that constructs its context.

r002.rationale: It calls policy a program and defines it as the whole system deciding what to do next, including the model and explicit surrounding structure.

r003.rationale: It says the agent can modify parts of its program, but does not describe self-improvement of machinery that defines skills or distinguish that from adding skills through existing extension points.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the "policy" isn't really the model weights. People hear "recursively self-improving" and immediately picture a model fine-tuning its own weights in a loop, and that's not what we're doing, at least not at first. The policy, in the sense that actually matters, is everything that sits around the model: the harness, the tool definitions, the prompts, the retrieval layer, the way context gets assembled, the eval suite that tells you whether a change was good. That whole bundle is what produces behavior, and that whole bundle is just code and text. Which means the agent can read it, reason about it, and propose diffs to it.

So the loop looks a lot more like a software engineering loop than an RL loop. The agent runs on a batch of tasks, some fraction of them fail, and instead of a human going "huh, it keeps forgetting to check the file exists before writing," the agent itself does the postmortem. It looks at the trajectory, forms a hypothesis about what in the harness let that failure happen, writes the change, and then it has to prove the change on held-out tasks before it merges. The eval gate is the thing I'd stress. Without that, "self-improving" just means "self-modifying," and those are very different words.

The reason I like framing it this way is that it keeps the improvement legible. If the agent changes a prompt or adds a tool, you can read the diff. You can revert it. You can see the eval numbers that justified it. Whereas if the improvement is buried in a weight update, you've lost all of that, and you've also lost the ability to have a human in the loop at the merge step, which for now I think is pretty important.

The honest caveat is that the ceiling on this approach is bounded by the base model. You can make the harness arbitrarily good, but at some point the model itself is the limiting factor, and then you do need to touch training. My bet is that there's a lot more headroom in the harness than people assume, and that the data you generate from an agent carefully editing its own scaffolding is exactly the kind of data you'd want when you eventually do train on it. So the two stages aren't in conflict. You do the legible version first, and it produces the material for the less legible version later.

r001.rationale: It describes the policy as the harness and surrounding machinery that assembles context and shapes behavior around the model.

r002.rationale: It says policy includes the whole bundle around the model and identifies that bundle as code and text the agent can inspect and change.

r003.rationale: It mentions changing the harness and adding tools, but does not explain that self-improvement reaches the machinery defining skills beyond using existing extension points.

astra-6.text:
I think of the agent policy as the thing that determines what the agent does next, given what it’s seen so far. That’s broader than just the model weights. It includes the instructions, the tools available to it, how it manages context, and how it decides whether to keep working or stop.

The idea behind recursive self-improvement is to let the agent work on that policy itself. It can look at a trajectory, identify where it made a bad decision, propose a change, and test whether that change actually helps. And the process it uses to propose and evaluate those changes is itself part of the policy, so that can improve too.

The crucial distinction is between changing yourself and improving yourself. You need feedback that lets you tell whether a new policy performs better, rather than just producing a more convincing explanation of why it should.

r001.rationale: It lists instructions, tools, and context management as parts of the policy, but does not describe the agent as an LM call wrapped in machinery that constructs its context.

r002.rationale: It says the policy is broader than model weights and names several components, but does not define it as encompassing the entire code implementation.

r003.rationale: It discusses improving the policy and its evaluation process, but does not mention skill-defining machinery or extending beyond existing skill extension points.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the agent policy as the whole system that determines what an agent does next. Given a goal, its history, and the tools it has available, how does it choose an action? That includes the model, but also the prompts, the context you give it, and the code that orchestrates those decisions.

The way I conceptualize recursive self-improvement is that this policy can itself become something the agent works on. It can look at a trajectory, identify where it made a bad decision, propose a change, and test whether that change actually helps. If it does, that becomes the policy used for the next iteration—including the next attempt to improve the policy.

The hard part is closing that loop with a reliable measure of improvement. Making a change is easy. Establishing that it makes the agent better, rather than just better at the particular example it was looking at, is the important part.

r001.rationale: It describes the agent as a model operating with prompts, supplied context, and orchestration code that helps determine its next action.

r002.rationale: It includes code that orchestrates decisions, but does not clearly say the policy encompasses the agent’s entire code implementation.

r003.rationale: It says the policy can be revised and tested, but does not mention skill-defining machinery or extending beyond existing skill extension points.
